name: Pedro Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Pedro Khan, 43, a senior operator at a large mine. I check the dump body and the haul route, then move ore; I watch the load settle before I reverse, because a rushed turn can bend steel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what do you carry home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like doing the job properly and teaching a newer driver the right pace. My partner Claudia works at a pharmacy counter; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and around three months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small program can tally fuel use, but it cannot tell a new rattle from the loader's normal hum. I still use the hand signal before reversing toward the dump point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is operating equipment, and the card leaves pay much as it is. My partner Claudia works at a pharmacy counter, and we keep around three months of household bills aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the same loader checks and let the planner compare fuel totals for a month. I would wait before buying any new tool or changing our family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the work in this mild case. I know the pharmacy has busy seasons too, but our mortgage is covered with both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you want a supervisor to keep checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Claudia to check the monthly bill envelope with me before we postpone anything. We would delay the porch chairs first and keep the children's school and mortgage payments steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your partner to know before your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the fitter to compare the fuel summary with actual service notes. If it misses a fault, I would make sure the operator keeps the usual signed inspection.

say: I would let software tally **fuel use**, but not judge a new rattle.
I still use a clear **hand signal** when reversing.
think: Most of my day is **equipment work**, and pay stays much the same here.
I rely on two wages and a **three-month reserve**.
do: Keep the loader checks and compare a month of **fuel totals**.
Wait before buying tools or changing the **family budget**.
feel: I feel **settled** about the work, with both household wages covering the mortgage.
S0.quote: I still use the hand signal before reversing toward the dump point.
fieldNote: Pedro values familiar **loader checks** over a new tally.
His pharmacy-employed partner and **three-month reserve** support the household.
He expects little change to his own **income** in the plateau case.

steps.text: Keep the loader checks on every shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew software will take more buying and shift planning, while the loader remains hands-on for now. I would ask who checked the faster target before we are told to meet it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I assign operators and scan the repair schedule, so some senior desk duties could go. The haul work stays longer, but losing one planning shift would cut my overtime and I would notice it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the experienced drivers to test the route tool after the mine shows its training plan. I would take the mine's apprenticeship module for mobile equipment if it explains a real job, not just another screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a lost planning shift even if I still drive most days. Three months saved gives us a buffer, but not a reason to ignore income risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you want a supervisor to keep checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the supervisor to keep checking the weather, dump-point queues and new driver's hours. A screen can shorten a route and still leave a crew in a risky place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your partner to know before your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need one of the operators to show me the tool working on an ordinary and a messy shift. I would use it only after we could explain why it sends the truck a certain way.

say: I expect software to take more **buying and planning**, while loader work stays hands-on for now.
I would ask who checked the faster **target**.
think: I expect haul work to last three more years after the **shift board** changes.
I worry losing a planning shift would cut my **overtime**.
do: Ask experienced drivers to test the route tool after **training**.
Take the mobile-equipment **apprenticeship module** if it leads to a job.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost planning hours despite the hands-on work.
S1.quote: The haul work stays longer, but losing one planning shift would cut my overtime and I would notice it at home.
fieldNote: The route tool could affect his **lead duties** before loader operation.

steps.text: Test the route tool with experienced drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could handle the shift board by 2028, while loader robots come around 2031. The mine should tell people which physical jobs still have hours before anyone borrows to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose allocation work first and then face robots taking loader shifts three years later. I use AI after seeing others try it, but full AGI makes a screen-based transfer a poor fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office now whether it has a paid mobile-equipment apprenticeship. In 2029, I would start it if the mine reserved a field placement, and I would keep my current shifts until the placement began.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels quick, and I am anxious that my overtime could shrink before the course starts. We have a reserve and Claudia's wages, but I do not want to waste either on an unrecognized class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you want a supervisor to keep checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claudia and I would compare the course calendar with the pharmacy rota and mortgage date. I would not use savings unless the mine named the placement and covered the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your partner to know before your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no paid placement appeared in 2029, I would keep driving and ask to join the next apprenticeship intake. I would look at nearby mine jobs before paying out of pocket.

say: I expect AGI to handle shift boards by **2028**, with loader robots around 2031.
I want a list of jobs with **physical hours** before retraining.
think: I could lose allocations before loader robots take **shifts**.
I see a screen-based role as poor fallback after full **AGI**.
do: Ask now whether the mine offers a paid mobile-equipment **apprenticeship**.
Start in 2029 if the mine reserves a **field placement**.
feel: Two years feels **quick**, and I worry overtime could shrink before training starts.
S2.quote: I use AI after seeing others try it, but full AGI makes a screen-based transfer a poor fallback.
fieldNote: Pedro seeks a practical apprenticeship rather than a **screen transfer**.
The three-year **robot lag** gives him time only if a placement is available.
Claudia’s rota and mortgage timing shape his **study schedule**.

steps.text: Request the mine mobile-equipment apprenticeship details

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to train before AGI in 2031. Robots reach loader work around 2034, so a mine should show which trade posts are still funded by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shift board can change early, while loader work lasts longer. I could learn to service the large dump bodies, but robots may eventually do those repairs too, so I would not call it safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd complete the mine's dump-body service apprenticeship over the next few years and ask for a supervised repair shift. In 2032, I would apply for a funded service role if the work still involved physical equipment, keeping my loader job until an offer was firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about where the job ends up, but five years lets me make a more sensible move. I would feel worse if I had to choose between the mortgage and a course fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you want a supervisor to keep checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to know whether technicians still work underneath the body or mainly approve automated reports. That difference matters more to me than the job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your partner to know before your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would ask the maintenance lead for the actual service duties and apply if people were still needed on site. If not, I would keep operating and check vacancies at another mine.

say: I see five years to train before AGI in **2031**.
I want to know which trade posts remain funded after robots around **2034**.
think: I expect the shift board to change before loader work, and I would ask about **2034**.
Dump-body service is not safe forever if robots take the **repairs**.
do: Complete the dump-body service **apprenticeship** and request a repair shift.
Apply in 2032 for a funded job with physical **equipment duties**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years lets me plan more sensibly.
S3.quote: I could learn to service the large dump bodies, but robots may eventually do those repairs too, so I would not call it safe forever.
fieldNote: He wants a concrete dump-body skill, while acknowledging later **robot exposure**.
Pedro would compare job duties with **technology**, not trust the title.
He will not leave loader pay before a **funded offer**.

steps.text: Apply for a funded repair post in 2032
Keep operating until the repair offer is firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years is useful if the mine releases dates early. AGI arrives in 2036 and robots reach loader work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 at AGI and 56 when robots follow, and still need regular pay. I could move to dump-body service, but that work might also be automated before I finish paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader shift while finishing the service apprenticeship and put a fixed amount from each pay into savings. In 2037, I would apply for a service post only if the mine confirmed the position was funded beyond the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer notice gives me time, but I am still uneasy about wages after 2039. Three months saved will help with a short change, not a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you want a supervisor to keep checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, the children will be young adults, and Claudia and I would ask what work they want before paying for training. I would encourage them to learn a trade that can be used at more than one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your partner to know before your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the mine's service plan with openings at two nearby sites before deciding about a move. I would not change our home or school until I had a signed offer and a budget for travel.

say: I think ten years is useful if the mine releases **dates** early.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need **regular pay**.
Dump-body service might also be automated before the mortgage is **paid**.
do: Finish the service apprenticeship while keeping my **loader shift**.
Save from each pay and apply in 2037 for a funded **service post**.
feel: The longer notice helps, but I remain **uneasy** about wages after 2039.
S4.quote: Three months saved will help with a short change, not a long gap.
fieldNote: Pedro plans training without assuming **service work** will remain human-led.
He expects his children to be young adults by **2037** and asks their preferences.
A funded **multi-year post** is his condition for changing sites.

steps.text: Finish the dump-body service apprenticeship while operating

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me because the shift board changes before the robots arrive. Paid apprenticeship places, a named job at the end and enough notice for family schedules would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want a course linked to a real job and a fair chance to apply for it. A hard-working family should not have to choose between a mortgage payment and training that goes nowhere.

headlineQuote: A hard-working family should not have to choose between a mortgage payment and training that goes nowhere.
portrait: Pedro is a 43-year-old senior operator at a large mine with a **technical diploma**.
He prefers proven routines and learns technology after others **show it works**.
His partner works at a pharmacy; their mortgage and **three-month reserve** shape decisions.
He favors apprenticeship and family work choices but does not assume any service job is safe from **robots**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him because shift planning could change before an apprenticeship begins.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships**, a named job and family notice would help Pedro plan.
